entry.title: Hedging Against Misspecification
entry.content:
Which actions reveal the most information about a hidden variable? And can we trust those actions when our notion of “informativeness” itself depends on imperfect beliefs? To address these questions, I aim to provide an informal introduction to the framework of Bayesian experimental design (BED) and its recent evolution under deep learning. This draws partly on research I conducted for my MSc dissertation, but I hope to broaden the discussion toward the end with connections to world models. Code for the experiments is available in the GitHub repository.

Bayesian experimental design

At its core, BED offers principled decision criteria for choosing actions or experimental designs that maximally reduce our uncertainty about a fixed but unknown parameter \(\theta^*\). Since \(\theta^*\) is unknown, we introduce a random variable \(\theta\) in its place and encode our beliefs about its value in a prior \(p(\theta)\). The experiment is assumed to generate an observable outcome \(y\) that depends on \(\theta^*\) and our chosen design \(\xi\) according to the likelihood \(p(y \mid \theta^*, \xi)\). We then use this outcome to update our beliefs about \(\theta^*\) using Bayes’ rule:

\[\begin{aligned} p(\theta \mid y, \xi) &= \frac{p(y \mid \theta, \xi)\, p(\theta)}{p(y \mid \xi)}, \\[4pt] \text{where} \quad p(y \mid \xi) &:= \int p(y \mid \theta, \xi)\, p(\theta)\, \mathrm{d}\theta. \end{aligned}\]

In other words, the posterior upweights values of \(\theta\) in the support of the prior for which the observed outcome \(y\) has higher likelihood. Assuming the likelihood is well-specified and \(\theta^*\) lies within the support of our prior, the posterior tends to concentrate around the true value \(\theta^*\) (Kleijn & van der Vaart, 2012). The interesting question is then: which design \(\xi\) leads to the greatest concentration of our beliefs around the truth—that is, which is most informative?
